title: If you find anything better
hookLine: if you find anything better than justice, truth, self-control and courage, turn to it; if not, make room for nothing else (Meditations 3.6)

cards: Most advice tells you what to want. Marcus Aurelius does something stranger: he issues a challenge, aimed at himself. Go ahead, he says.
Search all of human life. If you find something better than these four things, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy it. He isn't defending a position.
He's daring himself to beat it. An emperor who could have anything, asking what's actually worth having. Today: if you find anything better.

teach.h: THE FOUR: JUSTICE, TRUTH, CONTROL, COURAGE.
teach.b: The four are justice, truth, self-control and courage. Readers of Plato will hear the old Greek list of four virtues, where wisdom usually stands.
Marcus puts truth in that place, which tells you something about him: for a man surrounded by flatterers, truth was a daily discipline. Then the dare.

If you find anything better than these, turn to it. He raises the stakes: if you find anything better than the guiding spirit inside you, the reason that governs your choices and keeps you honest, take that instead.
And he answers himself. If nothing better turns up, and he expects nothing will, make room for nothing else.
Next come the rivals that usually crowd in: praise from the crowd, power, wealth, the enjoyment of pleasures. He doesn't call them evil. His worry is subtler.
Let one sit beside the four as an equal, even briefly, and it starts to take over without asking. A second loyalty quietly becomes the first.
So, he writes, simply and freely choose the better, and hold on to it. Not a long calculation every morning, weighing virtue against convenience. One plain choice, then kept.
And it gives any day four questions. Was I fair?
Was I true? Did I hold back where I needed to? Did I do the hard thing?

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use the four virtues of Meditations 3.6 as an evening check: was I just, truthful, self-controlled and brave today?

o: keeping your feelings hidden so nobody can read them
holding yourself back where you need to, one of the four goods
being harsh with yourself whenever you make a mistake

s: Marcus forbids looking for anything better than the four
he dares himself to look: if you find something better, he says, turn to it.
Marcus worries that rivals like praise slowly take over
let one sit beside the four as an equal, and it starts to take the lead.
Marcus calls wealth and pleasure evil in this passage
his worry is that they compete with the good, not that they are evil.

games.q: a new job pays far more, but you'd have to shade the truth to clients every day. what fits Meditations 3.6?
o: take it: money is a kind of good too.
weigh it against the four, and choose simply.
take it, and promise to be honest later.
games.why: Marcus asks whether anything is better than justice and truth; if not, it gets no room beside them.

practice: Walk back through your day so far, or yesterday if it's early, and find one moment for each of the four: being fair, being true, holding back, doing the uncomfortable thing. Don't grade too hard.
Just notice which got the most room, and which got crowded out.

wordCard.voice: Self-control. One of the four goods in Marcus's dare, alongside justice, truth and courage: if you find anything better, turn to it. If not, give room to nothing else. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'sound-mindedness': self-control, one of the four goods Marcus names in 3.6.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing better. One plain choice, made simply, then kept. Day five hundred forty-two, done.
